https://www.politico.eu/article/elon-mus.text: Owner of X and world’s first trillionaire Elon Musk attacked French presidential candidate Marine Tondelier on Thursday, after the Greens party leader said French authorities should be able to suspend the platform during electoral campaigns in case of foreign interference. “I demand that she be shut down for treason against France!” Musk wrote on X, prompting a strong reaction from Tondelier. “France does not need lessons in patriotism from a foreign billionaire who thinks he gets to decide which European political leaders should be silenced. Democracy is not for sale. Not even to the richest man in the world,” she responded . Advertisement Advertisement “I’d rather be accused of defending democracy than of trying to buy it.” Musk, who is a former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump, has regularly weighed in on European politics and thrown his support behind far-right candidates and parties — and France is no exception. In July, Musk said far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen was “France’s last hope,” but her National Rally party was quick to downplay his backing to avoid being associated with the controversial owner of Tesla and SpaceX. Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon also slammed Musk’s attacks against Tondelier on Thursday, before accusing the French government of not doing enough to fight foreign interference. “The French presidential election is an open bar for all the manipulators in the world,” he wrote — a criticism Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot promptly rejected . Earlier this week, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government was boosting efforts to detect and punish foreign interference in the upcoming 2027 election, while presidential candidates Gabriel Attal and Édouard Philippe , as well as likely candidate Raphaël Glucksmann shared they had been victims of Russian disinformation campaigns. https://www.politico.eu/article/hungary-.text: PRAGUE— Hungary said Thursday it is on track to rejoin the EU's flagship research program, Horizon Europe, potentially unlocking millions in European funding that had been blocked under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Hungarian Science and Tech Minister Zoltán Tanács told POLITICO that all legal barriers to accessing EU research funding have been cleared by changing how its higher education is governed, meeting the technical criteria agreed upon with Brussels. "Legally, we are back again," Tanács said, speaking on the sidelines of the Central and Eastern Europe Artificial Intelligence Summit in Prague. "We have restructured our university management. We have eliminated all those strange structures that have been set up by the former government." Advertisement Advertisement A European Commission spokesperson said Brussels has "not been formally notified yet" by Hungary. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in late May, during a meeting with new Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, that the country would be "gradually phasing out" the so-called public-interest trusts, a series of asset-management foundations set up by the Orbán government to control parts of how higher education was administered. Those trusts raised conflict-of-interest concerns and triggered a 2022 EU decision to shut Hungary out of many of the Europe-funded research projects. Hungary being locked out of the EU's €95 billion research program Horizon Europe "created huge damage," Tanács said. Asked about the timing to access the funding, he said there was still some "administration" to be done, but he was confident that Brussels would unlock the funds by the end of the year and rejoin both Horizon Europe and the higher-education program Erasmus+. Since his resounding April victory, Magyar has pushed to bring Hungary back into the EU fold and tap into European funding that had largely dried up during the latter phase of Orbán's nearly two decades in power, marked by open conflict with Brussels. Hungary has touted its ambitions to invest heavily in artificial intelligence for whenever access to European research collaboration is restored. "We want to establish hundreds of new AI professorships that can be done internationally," Tanács said. Advertisement Advertisement

https://blabbermouth.net/features/the-ba.text: The Battle Between Metal And Orchestra Still Goes On For SEPTICFLESH October 6, 2026 By David E. Gehlke SEPTICFLESH and an orchestra are now inseparable. The long-running Greek extreme metal outfit has taken a union that was originally popularized by the likes of CRADLE OF FILTH , DIMMU BORGIR and even METALLICA , via 1999's "S&M" , making it such an integral part of their core sound that it's difficult to imagine that they will record future releases without some kind of cooperation from a symphony. The results speak for themselves, too. Starting with their brilliant 2008 comeback album, "Communion" , SEPTICFLESH doesn't use an orchestra as an adornment — they use it as a feature, with sweeping arrangements and moments of sheer grandiosity that fire alongside extreme metal flourishes and Spiros Antoniou 's prominent, guttural vocals. It's all made possible by Spiros 's brother, Christos , who studied composition at the London College Of Music and now is a professional composer. Circa 2026, the Greeks are hard at work on a new studio album to follow up 2022's "Modern Primitive" and have recently performed with the Plovdiv Philharmonic Orchestra and the National Opera Choir Of Plovdiv in Plovdiv, Bulgaria. In the more immediate future, SEPTICFLESH will be trekking across North America with ARCH ENEMY and THE BLACK DAHLIA MURDER this fall, a reminder of how far the band has come since their formative melodic black/death years in the mid-1990s to their controversial detour in 1999 with " Revolution DNA" . Christos Antoniou is here to bring BLABBERMOUTH.NET up to speed. (Note: This interview was conducted weeks before the announcement that Antoniou would not join his bandmates on their North American tour due to an injury.) Blabbermouth : SEPTICFLESH went on hiatus for three years, then came back in 2007. Looking back, how beneficial was it for the band? Christos : "I think it was a wise decision. We were a bit lacking with the release of ' Sumerian Daemons' because the label, at the time [ Hammerheart Records ], had some issues with DEATH , Chuck Schuldiner . I don't know the real reasons, but the label went bankrupt. [Author's note: In 2003, Schuldiner 's family blocked Hammerheart from releasing the unfinished second album demos from Schuldiner 's CONTROL DENIED , leading to a costly court battle.] We sat down and said it was time to take a break; I also had work in England as a composer at Pinewood Studios . My brother was focused on album covers for metal bands. Sotiris [ Vayenas , guitar] had his own work. It was a decision, as I said before, and as SEPTICFLESH , when we release something, it has to be important for us. We just don't want to release an album to say we released an album. We didn't have anything to offer our listeners at the time. I think this break played an important role. It was a positive act, for sure." Blabbermouth : So it was more of a business decision than anything? Did you not get the support you needed behind that record? `Christos : "Money's not the most important thing. The most important thing is to have the desire, the fire. As I said, the vision there was destroyed in a way. It's important for an artist to have a vision and the fire that will let him create. Suddenly, we didn't have this fire. It's not about money. It's about soul. We felt that the right decision was to take a break. Of course, during that time, we didn't know we would return. [ Laughs ] It was the final chapter for us, 'Sumerian Daemons' . The circumstances led the band to return with 'Communion' ." Blabbermouth : How do you view "Sumerian Daemons" now? Do you see it as the band's musical turning point? Christos : "We always try to experiment and to find a new way to suggest colors, new sound — a fresh sound. After 'Revolution DNA' , we said it was time to become more aggressive. We don't regret 'Revolution DNA' . I think 'Revolution DNA' was 1998 and 'Sumerian' was 2002. During that time, we felt that our composition process was more aggressive, more experimental and more brutal, in a way. But I don't think 'Sumerian Daemons' is the most important album. I think the most important album was 'Communion' because it was the first time we had a serious label behind us [ Season Of Mist ]. It was the first time we had a live orchestra. We recorded in Prague with the Prague Philharmonic Orchestra , and it was the first time managers and agencies approached us. This was the turning point for us. We don't regret our past. Many people say, 'Why don't you play songs from your past?' We're about the future. We are looking forward. The sound of SEPTICFLESH today has the sound of the orchestra." Blabbermouth : If memory serves, the response to "Communion" was overwhelmingly positive. Christos : "When we said that we are going to form the band again, we said, 'Take it easy. We don't have to be anxious. Let the things go on and see how it goes.' Gradually, we saw all of this positive feedback. We saw a big difference with a label that had bigger distribution channels. Gradually, things kept getting better and better. With 'Communion' , we started to do big tours. We did a European tour with CRADLE OF FILTH , MOONSPELL and GORGOROTH . Then, we went to the States for the first time in 2009 with CRADLE OF FILTH and SATYRICON . Things started to get serious. We were really happy about this. We said that 'Now it's our moment. We need to follow this momentum.'" Blabbermouth : How much of your education helped when writing songs like "Anubis" ? Christos : "We were beginners with 'Communion' in terms of the battle between metal and the orchestra. Although I had started classical music composition and orchestration, the battle still goes on. [ Laughs ] We're still learning. The most important thing is to give the orchestral and metal fields space to breathe and not conflict with each other. This is a big headache for our producer, but during 'Communion' , the sound is more raw. We were still adapting the orchestra. Gradually, after 'The Great Mass' , 'Titan' , 'Codex Omega' , we've reached a moment where sometimes we have to be more careful with how metal and the orchestration blend. With 'Communion' , we didn't have this experience. Of course, the material is more raw. It's different, 'Communion' , than 'Modern Primitive' or 'The Great Mass' . We're still learning. We were still learning. We did a good job, though, but there was always room for progress." Blabbermouth : What kind of reactions did you get from people within the orchestral world when they discovered you're in an extreme metal band? Did anyone give you a hard time? Christos : "If you are a conservative person, then yes. Nowadays, metal is everywhere. It's good that our music is everywhere. If you are conservative, of course you will find it strange that someone who listens to metal also listens to classical music and does film scores. I think nowadays, it's not so common. For example, in Athens, we played with the biggest orchestra in Athens at the Acropolis. Most people there really enjoyed it. Of course, some people will be against it. They are blind and conservative. When you are conservative, you have many limits. You will think our music is Satanic; we don't have any connection with that. My brother's voice, to someone, will sound a bit like a dog. [ Laughs ] I think we're in 2026, and things are getting better. Crossover projects are everywhere." Blabbermouth : Do you have to flip the switch on either one of these? Or do you live in both worlds? Christos : "I'm myself. I don't change face when I compose classical music, or when I'm playing music for SEPTICFLESH . I'm the same guy. I don't have to switch. I'm an introverted guy who studies this work when I have to compose music. It's the same as when I study, using it as a reference to write for SEPTICFLESH . For me, music is the most important thing. It doesn't matter if it's classical or metal. The fire, as I said, has driven me to compose music for metal, classical music and concert music." Blabbermouth : Is this all you do? Christos : "Yes. I'm a professional composer. When I write a song for SEPTICFLESH , I don't write it as a songwriter. Maybe that is a difference I took from the concert music world. I take the work as a composition. It's different because I always have to study. I want my sound to evolve. On the other hand, my brother, Sotiris , Krimh [drummer Kerim Lechner ], when they write music, have their own agenda. Mine is this. It's totally different. They have to compromise because I deliver the most complex things to them. [ Laughs ] They get worried sometimes. We have a good relationship. We have found the formula that we know works. 'Communion' , if we take a song that is very complex, like 'Babel's Gate' . It was a strange situation. [Ex-drummer] Fortis [ Benardo ] had to take a score for months to memorize the pattern. Nowadays, it's getting easier. They know how I work. I know how they work. They give me their parts; I orchestrate; I add some of my style. On the contrary, I give them my orchestral motifs, and then we'll make the metal parts. We work like that." Blabbermouth : You and your brother have been doing this for so long. Do you guys ever fight? Christos : "We fight so much. [ Laughs ] If he weren't my brother, we wouldn't be in the same band. [ Laughs ] Maybe many other bands have this, but because we are brothers, we continue." Blabbermouth : Can you tell what the other is thinking? Christos : "Of course, but that doesn't change our minds. You know when a fight is coming. Our bandmates know how to deal with it." Blabbermouth : You've always had a strong lineup. I'm sure that helps whenever there are any dustups. Christos : " Sotiris has been with us from the beginning. We are the backbone of SEPTICFLESH . We have never changed the original members. This is a plus. I would say we are like a factory. Everything has to be delivered from our factory to the label. My brother does the art and cover. Sotiris does the lyrics. I am on the classical side. All of us compose. I also want to mention that Krimh does excellent work. We take releasing albums very seriously. The biggest trouble for an artist is not to repeat himself. We have so many minds that provide ideas; it helps us. On the contrary, a person who is alone might be drained because you don't know when you are repeating yourself. You have to follow your inspiration and filter out what's best for you. This is a common mistake for artists. They repeat themselves. I'm not saying you have to play jazz, but you have to experiment. Knowledge is power. You have to develop your sound. Always." Blabbermouth : Speaking of which, how is the new album coming along? Christos : "We are nearly at the end of our compositional process. It's getting faster. Each of these songs needs to find its own shape. Things will change when we add vocals and lyrics, and when we go into the studio; I will be in Prague. Before the mixing, things will change a lot. At the moment, we have 50 percent of the new album." Blabbermouth : How does it compare to "Modern Primitive" ? Christos : "I know it's faster, but it doesn't mean the number of beats, the tempo, the BPM. It's more about how you will blend the dark moments with the fast elements. At the moment, it looks more brutal for sure." Photograph: Visit Norway Norway ‘We make shit houses great again’: Visit Norway cleans up after Trump’s insult Tourist board responds with toilet humour after US president expresses ire over failure to win Nobel peace prize, labelling it a ‘shithouse country’ Jon Henley Europe correspondent Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.22 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Some might find it decidedly incommodious to be dumped on by Donald Trump as a “shithouse country”. Not the Norwegian tourist board, which chose instead to lift the lid on some of the nation’s loveliest lavatories. “Are these the world’s best shit houses?” asked Visit Norway on its website , days after the US president vented his fury once more over failing to win the Nobel peace prize by describing Norway as a “shithouse country” at a rally on Sunday. “Norway makes shit houses great again!” the agency continued above pictures of some of the country’s most striking public conveniences, adding: “These toilets are worth a visit, both when you really have to go – and when you don’t.” View image in fullscreen At Ostasteidn in Ryfylke, the restroom is designed so that moss will start to grow on the outer walls, like camouflage. Photograph: Vist Norway Trump delivered his tirade at a rally in Michigan days before the US midterm elections. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually,” he declared, using a term he has previously applied to Haiti, ​Libya, Somalia and Yemen. He added that he would welcome migrants from some countries but not Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize”. Earlier this month, Trump denounced the decision to award the prize to Navi Pillay, a former ⁠international criminal court judge. “This is an indelible stain on the ‌country ⁠of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” he said. “I never heard of this person. The ⁠Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited … And we will ​not forget, Norway.” Along 18 designated scenic routes around Norway, Visit Norway said, leading architects had been tasked with transforming the humble wayside privy into an attraction in its own right. Several have since won international architecture awards. View image in fullscreen A toilet at Allmannajuvet in Sauda, Norway. Photograph: Andreas Solbakken/Vist Norway The agency pictured a series of designer public conveniences, many of them architecturally striking and all offering breathtaking vistas overlooking fjords, beside rushing rivers and foaming waterfalls, and at stunning scenic viewpoints. They “invite you to take your time and enjoy the scenery, even if you don’t have any business to take care of”, Visit Norway said, highlighting – among others – the restrooms at the Stegastein viewpoint in the Sognefjord region of western Norway. This particular comfort station, the tourist board noted with uninhibited pride, had been ranked among the 10 best public toilets in the world by DesignCurial, the online architecture, design and interiors magazine. Combining clean, minimalist lines with the fjord’s rugged and brooding landscape, the loos are famous for their large, black-tinted glass windows, which allow visitors a sweeping view from the throne while remaining invisible from the outside. View image in fullscreen The ‘golden toilet’ at Ersfjordstranda in Senja. Photograph: Hugo Fagermo/Foto: Hugo Fagermo It also highlighted the unique, wave-shaped Ureddplassen loo on the wild coast of Helgeland, the southernmost district of northern Norway, hailed by several international publications as the most scenic restroom in the world. Also featured are the solar-powered modernist bog at the Utsikten viewpoint, the “Instagram-worthy” Tungeneset loo (“looks pretty good underneath the northern lights”), and the world-famous triangular “golden toilet” on Senja island. Jens Kjeldsen, a rhetoric professor at the University of Bergen, said that under the circumstances, Visit Norway’s response was well judged. “It’s like the bully in kindergarten,” he told NRK public television . “If you get too serious, the bully wins.” View image in fullscreen Uredd Rest Area (Ureddplassen) on the Helgeland coast. Photograph: Steinar Skaar/Steinar Skaar, Statens vegvesen Evgenia Egorova, a senior consultant at Visit Norway, told the broadcaster the response to its social media fightback had been immense. “The world needs a little laugh,” she said. “We thought: let’s meet them with kindness, and a little humour.” Visit Norway said it had more stylish loos in the pipeline, including a forest-inspired latrine using dried wood from more than 60 trees. “Get ready for the pit stop of your life,” it urged, before signing off with a cheery: “Toodeloo!” The Nobel peace prize is famously not awarded by the nation or even the government of Norway, but by the Nobel prize committee, which operates independently – something Trump “knows very well”, the foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said. “We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering.” View image in fullscreen The toilet at Eggum in Lofoten is built as an amphitheatre underneath the ruins of a German radar station.
